pages.text:
Stiff-Man Syndrome-80: A Variant Associated with
Abnormal Visual Processing and a New Antineuronal
Antibody
Robert B. Darnell, Michael Ruhin, Jonathan Victor,
and Fred Phm, New York, NY
Stiff-man syndrome (SMS) is associated with the production
of an autoantibody specific for a 60-kd species of glutamic
acid decarboxylase (GAD) (Solimena et al, N Engl J Med
1988;318:1012). We studied a 37-year-old man with a diag-
nosis of SMS based on symptoms of progressive stiffness,
chiefly in the lower extremities and relieved by diazepam,
and characteristic EMG findings. Visual evoked potentials
(VEPs) were abnormal bilaterally (P100 was 123 msec OU,
normal population mean + 2 SD = 109 msec), and nor-
malized after administration of diazepam. The physiological
abnormalities in SMS associated with GABAergic dysfunc-
tion are not confined to the motor system; further, VEPs
may aid in the diagnosis and classification of SMS. Immu-
nohistochemical analysis using the patient’s serum or CSF
demonstrated neuronal binding identical to that reported

with anti-GAD antibodies. Western blot analysis revealed
immunoreactivity to an 80-kd antigen present in human Pur-
kinje and neocortical cell extracts; the 60-kd antigen elicited
no reactivity. Of note, an 80-kd species of GAD has been
reported in rat brain (Denner et al, PNAS 1987;84:668). We
propose that this man harbors an anti-GAD antibody with
specificity distinct from that previously reported. SMS may
represent a spectrum of autoimmune disease with antibodies
generated against different species of the GAD enzyme.
Neuronotrophic Factor Rescue of Toxic Neuropathy
Stuart C. Apfl, Richard B. Lipton, Joseph C. Awezo, and
John A. Kessler, Bronx, NY
Neuropathy is the dose-limiting toxicity for a number of
important therapeutic agents. For example, the new anti-
tumor drug, taxol, causes a painful sensory neuropathy at
therapeutic doses (Lipton RB, et al, Neurology 1989;
39:368-371). In this study we established a mouse model
of taxol-induced neuropathy and examined the effects of
coadministration of nerve growth factor (NGF). Mice were
injected with taxol, taxol plus NGF, or vehicle, and were
examined for behavioral, biochemical, and electrophysiolog-
ical manifestations of neuropathy. Taxol administration
significantly @ < 0.001) elevated the mean tailflick thresh-
old, a behavioral measure of nociception. Coadministra-
tion of NGP with taxol completely prevented any
change in the tailflick threshold. Taxol administration also
reduced levels of the peptide neurotransmitter, substance Y
(SP), in the C6 dorsal root ganglion to 12% of control (p <
0.001). Coadministration of NGF completely prevented this
decrease. Finally, electrical stimulation of the caudal nerve
was measured in the tail. Treatment with taxol reduced the
compound nerve amplitudes by 25% (p < 0.05), and coad-
ministration of NGF completely prevented this decrease.
These results indicate that NGF is capable of preventing
taxol neuropathy in mice. We are currently investigating
other neurotoxins and neuronotrophic factors using these
measures. The striking protective effect of NGF in prevent-
ing taxol neuropathy in mice dictates a trial in patients receiv-
ing taxol as a chemotherapeutic agent.
Development of a Herpes Simplex Virus-mediated
Gene Transfer Latency Vector
David J. Fink, Marina Mata, Lmy Sternberg, William Goins,
and Joseph C. Glorioso, Ann Arbor, MI, and Pittsburgh, PA
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) establishes life-long latent in-
fections within neurons, characterized by the exclusive pro-
duction of latency-associated transcripts (LATs) and the com-
plete absence of viral lytic gene expression. We have
exploited these attributes to engineer recombinant HSV of
reduced neuropathogenicity carrying recombinant gene cas-
settes to serve as vectors for the transfer and expression of
foreign genes in the mature central nervous system. The E.
colz P-galactosidase (@-gal) gene (lacZ) was used as a reporter
foreign gene, driven by a viral late gene (gC) promoter or the
latency-active (LAT) promoter to indicate productive and
latent infection respectively. The recombinant HSV vectors
were stereotactically injected into hippocampus. Viral pro-
tein kinase (US3 )-deficient pgC:lacZ recombinants expressed
&gal in dentate gyrus neurons of the injected hippocampus
from 2 to 5 days after injection. Unlike wild-type virus, this
recombinant vector neither caused focal brain destruction
nor spread throughout brain. Following hippocampal inocu-
lation ICP4-deficient pLAT:lacZ recombinants, which tran-
siently express viral immediate early genes but are unable to
replicate, expressed @-gal in a number of cells throughout
the brain at times consistent with viral latency. This vector is
completely apathogenic. These results demonstrate the po-
tential utility of HSV vectors to express foreign genes in
brain cells.
